extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, and literary critics or students of poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative standards for composing and judging epic and tragic poetry (meter, scale, diction, use of the wonderful/irrational, and resolutions of critical difficulties) according to classical poetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale/length requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning and the end must be capable of being brought within a single view; the poem's scale should permit the whole to be grasped at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits epic poetry: poems smaller than old epics are acceptable (e.g., groups of tragedies presented at a single sitting). Epic, though able to enlarge dimensions, must retain a comprehensible beginning and end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of imitation: epic vs tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy must confine itself to the action on the stage and the part taken by players; epic, owing to the narrative form, can present many simultaneous events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic's narrative form allows episodes and simultaneous actions that add mass and dignity; tragedy cannot imitate several lines of action at once on stage without causing confusion or satiety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate metre for epic
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroic measure is the fitting and stateliest metre for epic; other metres would be incongruous on a great scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heroic metre admits rare words and metaphors and is 'stately' and 'massive.' Iambic and trochaic tetrameter are more stirring/action-like; mixing different metres (an anti-pattern) is absurd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mix metres
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing different metres in a poem (especially on a great scale) is inappropriate and incongruous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chaeremon's mixing is given as a negative example; nature (experience) teaches the proper measure — epic on a great scale has always used heroic verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's personal speech should be minimal
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person; imitation requires the poet to let characters act and speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homer is praised for immediately bringing in persons with characteristic qualities rather than appearing in person; over-authorial intrusion diminishes imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element of the wonderful/irrational
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy requires the wonderful; epic has wider scope for irrational elements because actors are not seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The wonderful pleases hearers; however, the tragic plot must not be composed of irrational parts—irrational elements should ideally lie outside the action (or be excluded). If introduced, they must be made plausible (an air of likelihood).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing incidents, a probable impossibility (an impossible event made probable artistically) is preferable to an improbable yet possible occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art may justify an impossibility if it attains the end of the art; otherwise every kind of error should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude irrational incidents from central action
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrational elements should be kept outside the main action; they are censurable if they occur within the drama without necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hero's ignorance that does not affect stage action may be tolerable (Oedipus), but irrational inclusions inside the drama (messenger's account in Electra) are faults that should have been avoided in construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction appropriate to function
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction should be elaborated in pauses of action (where there is no expression of character or thought); in moments of character/thought, over-brilliant diction obscures them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use more elaborate language in narrative/pauses; avoid dazzling verbal display when conveying character or internal thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vehicle of expression and language modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Poet uses language (current terms, rare words, metaphors) and many modifications of language; standards of correctness vary within the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of words (rare vs current) and metaphorical usage must suit the poetic form and the effect desired. Heroic metre, for instance, 'admits rare words and metaphors.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Different standards of correctness across arts and within poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard of correctness is not the same in poetry as in politics or other arts; within poetry there are faults that touch its essence and faults that are accidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors from lack of capacity (essential) are more serious than accidental errors from wrong choice (e.g., minor technical inaccuracies in depicting a craft).

rubrics_metrics.name: Essentials vs accidental errors
rubrics_metrics.description: If a poet imitates something incorrectly through want of capacity, the error is inherent; if due to a wrong choice (technical inaccuracy), the error is accidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between errors that undermine the poetry's essence and those that do not; the latter are less damning and sometimes excusable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors justified only if they serve artistic ends
rubrics_metrics.description: If an impossible element is introduced, it may be justified if the end of the art (the intended effect) is thereby attained; if the same end could be achieved without violating poetic rules, the error is not justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: pursuit of Hector may violate plausibility on stage but serve epic effect; still, avoid errors unless necessary for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation: consider context of acts/sayings
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging whether a saying or act is poetically right, consider who says it, to whom, when, by what means, and for what end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge isolated acts out of context — the intention and context may make them appropriate (e.g., to secure a greater good or avert a greater evil).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve critical difficulties by language analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Many textual or interpretive difficulties are solvable by reference to usage of language: accent/breathing, punctuation, ambiguity, dialectal meanings, metaphorical senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: accent or breathing distinctions, punctuation (Empedocles line), metaphor ('all' meaning 'many'), local usage (Cretan senses). These linguistic avenues often explain apparent faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreter's principle: prefer the poet's own text/assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Solve questions by reference to what the poet says himself or to what is tacitly assumed by an intelligent person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid critics' groundless inferences; consider alternative historical or textual traditions before condemning a passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five sources of critical objection
rubrics_metrics.description: Things are censured as: impossible, irrational, morally hurtful, contradictory, or contrary to artistic correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answers to objections should be sought under the twelve heads previously described (linguistic, contextual, formal, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrationality and depravity of character require inner necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrational actions or depravity of character are justly censured unless there is an inner necessity for their introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of unjustified irrationality or bad character: Aegeus in Euripides, Menelaus in Orestes — they are faults when not required by the plot's necessities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth: three objects of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must imitate one of three objects: things as they were/are, things as they are said or thought to be, or things as they ought to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permits different kinds of poetic 'truth' — factual, reputed, or idealized (Sophocles 'as they ought to be', Euripides 'as they are').

rubrics_metrics.name: Using reported/said forms to deflect objections
rubrics_metrics.description: If representation is neither true to fact nor ideal, the poet may claim to represent 'how men say the thing is' (e.g., tales about gods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an accepted defense for reports that are not factual: the poet represents common report or belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine apparent contradictions dialectically
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent contradictions should be examined as in dialectical refutation — whether the same thing is meant in the same relation and same sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve by reference to poet's wording or plausible tacit assumptions; do not leap to critics' groundless conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter/diction suitability determines admissible diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of metre influences admissible diction: the heroic metre readily admits rare words and metaphors, while other metres suit action or dancing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select words and metaphors compatible with chosen metre; avoid diction that clashes with the measure's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance/histrionic action should be judged by performer quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive gesture or bad action is a fault of performance, not necessarily of the poetic art; all action is not to be condemned, only bad or exaggerated action by poor performers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between defects of histrionic execution (gesture, twirling) and the inherent power of the poetic/tragic art, which can succeed by reading alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic ideal may surpass reality
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may represent idealized (even impossible) types when the ideal serves a higher artistic purpose; the impossible can be 'the higher thing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of idealization is defensible because the ideal type must sometimes surpass reality (Zeuxis example). Still, justify impossibility by reference to art's aims.
